Food companies marketing 'unhealthy' foods to children, says study | Australia news

Large food companies have set their standards for what constitutes healthy food so low that they consider products laden with fat, sugar and salt to be healthy and so continue to market them towards children, a Sydney study found.

Researchers from the Cancer Council NSW examined two weeks’ worth of food advertising broadcast between 6am and 9pm in Sydney by channels Seven, Nine and Ten to see how they rated for healthiness.

Food companies can currently use their own nutrition criteria to determine which foods can be marketed towards children and fast food outlets can sign up to a separate voluntary code.

But when assessed under a government-endorsed nutrition criteria, developed by Food Standards Australia New Zealand, the researchers found more than 60% of the 116 food advertisements targeted at children were considered unhealthy.

The study found foods such as Kellogg’s Coco Pops, Arnott’s Tiny Teddies and Nestle Smarties were promoted to children according to the food companies’ own voluntary health standards even though they would fail to be found healthy by the government regulators.

“We also found loopholes in the fast food code,” the council’s nutrition program manager and study author, Clare Hughes, said.

“Currently it only covers advertising of children’s meals, but our study found foods like KFC’s Mint Choc Krusher, and McDonald’s Chicken N’ Cheese Burger which aren’t children’s meals, can still be advertised to children.”

However, a spokesman for the Australian Food and Grocery Council said the research was not useful because the television advertising viewing window used by researchers did not reflect when children were watching programs.

“The research considers advertising during all shows between 6am to 9pm, covering crime programs like Law and Order and movies featuring sex and violence - programs which are hardly targeting children,” he said.

“This not a useful basis for which to consider advertising to children. It is disappointing that the paper did not consider that advertising bans overseas have demonstrated no reduction in childhood obesity.”

Hughes said there was no reason why the standards developed by Food Standards Australia and New Zealand should not be applied to food industry television advertising.

“Their system is the one that has been used to underpin food labelling regulations in Australia that now prevent companies from being able to make health claims such as ‘promotes healthy bones’,” she said.

“We should expect now that it has been applied to food packaging it should also be applied to television advertising to ensure unhealthy foods aren’t being promoted to children in other ways.”

A professor in health policy at Curtin University, Mike Daube, said the study, published in the journal Nutrition and Dietetics, was important, and that the food industry would always fight against strengthened marketing regulations.

“This study meticulously destroys the food industry’s phoney claims around responsible marketing,” Daube, who is also director of the Public Health Advocacy Institute, said.

“The food industry’s regulatory systems are designed to fail – and they fail especially to protect their youngest, most vulnerable consumers.

“In the 21st Century obesity era, their approach is utterly irresponsible – junk regulation for junk food marketing.”

Snack attack! Doritos and Coco Pops among latest products to shrink in UK | Food & drink industry

Doritos, Peperami and Coco Pops are the latest products to fall victim to shrinkflation as rising costs hit food producers.

The size of a large bag of Doritos has been reduced by 10% to 180g but remains on sale at the same average price of £1.99. A £1 “grab bag” is shrinking by nearly 12% to 90g.

Peperami has also shrunk by 10% to 22.5g while prices have remained steady at 79p a stick, or £1.59 for a pack of three. The price of the sausage sticks’ main ingredient, pork, hit a two-year high late last year amid high demand from China, while the fall in the pound has increased the cost of importing meat.

At the same time a big box of Coco Pops has been cut by 80g to 720g, but is selling for the same price of £3.75, and a smaller box has been reduced by 40g to 510g for the same price of £2.69.

Kellogg’s said the weight had dropped because it had cut the amount of sugar in its recipe. It said the number of Coco Pops in a box had actually increased by more than 10%. According to the Grocer trade journal, which first reported the weight change, the smaller box (reduced by 40g to 510g) now contains about 16,500 Coco Pops compared to about 14,500 previously, .

A spokesperson for Kellogg’s, the owner of Coco Pops, said: “We recently reduced sugar in Coco Pops Original by 14%, which has reduced the weight of some packs.

“By removing some of the sugar in the recipe and changing the coating, each Coco Pop weighs less than the previous recipe.”

The company, which has also cut the amount of sugar in Bran Flakes and Frosties, said it was doing so in response to demand from customers. In the case of Bran Flakes the pack weight didn’t change when the sugar was reduced, Kellogg’s said.

Lianne van den Bos, senior food analyst at Euromonitor International, said: “Many manufacturers will say that they are shrinking the size of their products as part of their responsibility to consumers with regards to health. But while this sounds honourable, the bottom line is the main motivation for shrinkflation.”

The latest round of shrinkflation – as the downsizing of favourite foods while holding the price has become known – follows similar moves by Maltesers, Hula Hoops and Toblerone.


The falling value of the pound since the Brexit vote has added to problems caused by the rising price of some commodities, such as butter and wheat.

Last week crisps and bacon were named as two of the products driving a sharp pick-up in food price inflation to 2.3% in the last three months, according to market research firm Kantar Worldpanel.

A spokesperson for Peperami said: “Peperami is manufactured in mainland Europe and has been subject to rising commodity costs and foreign exchange pressure due to significant currency fluctuations. We always endeavour to reduce the impact of such movements to ensure our brands are as affordable as possible for our loyal consumers.”

A spokesperson for Doritos owner PepsiCo said: “Like most businesses, we are facing factors such as fluctuating foreign exchange rates which are impacting the cost of ingredients and materials.

“As a result we’ve had to make a few changes to certain Doritos packs. We always strive to provide high quality, competitively priced products and will continue to review our range to ensure we offer great value to our customers.”

Kellogg's Coco Pops: The Ultimate Chocolatey Breakfast Cereal
 – McGrocer

Kellogg's Coco Pops have long been a staple in UK households, and for good reason. This chocolatey cereal brings joy to breakfast tables, and its unique flavor is loved by both kids and adults.

In this comprehensive review, we’ll dive deep into what makes Kellogg's Coco Pops so special, comparing them with other brands, analyzing their nutritional content, and considering their place in a balanced diet.

From the nostalgic taste to modern tweaks for healthier eating, we’ll cover it all. So grab your bowl and spoon, and let’s get started!


Introduction to Kellogg's Coco Pops

Kellogg's Coco Pops have been a beloved breakfast choice for decades. Their delicious chocolatey taste and crunchy texture make them a favorite among children and adults alike.

The cereal is made from puffed rice, coated with a sweet, chocolatey layer that turns milk into a delightful chocolate drink. It’s more than just a cereal; it’s an experience.


Taste and Texture Analysis

The taste of Kellogg's Coco Pops is unmistakably chocolatey. Each bite delivers a satisfying crunch, which softens just the right amount when mixed with milk.

Unlike some other chocolate cereals, Coco Pops maintain their texture well, giving you a delightful crunch from start to finish. It’s this perfect balance that keeps fans coming back.


Nutritional Information

Kellogg's Coco Pops are fortified with essential vitamins and minerals, including vitamin B12 and iron, making them a nutritious choice for breakfast. Each serving provides a balanced mix of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.

With recent trends towards healthier eating, Kellogg's has also introduced a version with 30% less sugar, making it a more health-conscious option without compromising on taste.


Comparison with Other Brands


Tesco Coco Pops

Tesco’s version of Coco Pops offers a similar chocolatey flavor but may lack the same crunch as Kellogg's. It's a more affordable option but might not satisfy the die-hard Coco Pops fans.


Aldi Coco Pops

Aldi’s Coco Pops are known for their budget-friendly price and decent taste. While they don’t quite match the Kellogg's original, they’re a good alternative for those looking to save a bit.


Lidl Coco Pops

Lidl’s offering is another low-cost version that mimics the chocolatey goodness of Kellogg's. It’s a close competitor in terms of taste and texture, making it a worthy contender.


Asda Coco Pops

Asda’s Coco Pops are popular for their rich chocolate flavor and crunchy texture. They provide a good balance between cost and quality, appealing to many households.


Kellogg's Coco Pops Loops

The Coco Pops Loops variant offers a fun twist on the classic with loop-shaped pieces. They have the same great taste and crunch, adding variety to your breakfast routine.


Kellogg's White Choc Coco Pops

For those who prefer white chocolate, Kellogg's White Choc Coco Pops are a delight. They bring a milder, creamier flavor while maintaining the beloved crunch.


Kellogg's Coco Pops Hazelnut Choc

This variant adds a nutty twist to the traditional chocolate flavor. The combination of hazelnut and chocolate makes for a rich and satisfying breakfast treat.


Price and Value for Money

When it comes to price, Kellogg's Coco Pops are positioned as a premium product. While they might be more expensive than store brands, the quality and taste justify the cost for many consumers.

For those on a budget, supermarket own-brand versions offer a reasonable alternative. However, the unique taste and texture of Kellogg's often make it worth the extra spend.


User Reviews and Feedback

User reviews for Kellogg's Coco Pops are overwhelmingly positive. Many highlight the nostalgic value, recalling fond childhood memories of enjoying this chocolatey cereal.

Parents appreciate the fortified vitamins and minerals, making it a guilt-free choice for their kids. The introduction of a lower sugar version has also received praise from health-conscious consumers.


Health Considerations

While Kellogg's Coco Pops are a tasty and fun breakfast option, it’s important to enjoy them as part of a balanced diet. The fortified vitamins and minerals provide essential nutrients, but the sugar content should be considered.

The lower sugar variant is a great option for those looking to reduce their sugar intake without sacrificing the beloved chocolatey taste. Pairing Coco Pops with a source of protein, like milk or yogurt, can help balance the meal.


Final Verdict and Recommendations

Kellogg's Coco Pops remain a top choice for a chocolatey breakfast cereal. Their unique taste, satisfying crunch, and nutritional fortifications make them a great option for families.

While there are more affordable alternatives available, the quality and nostalgia of Kellogg's Coco Pops often make them worth the premium price. Whether you’re a long-time fan or new to this classic, Coco Pops are sure to bring joy to your breakfast table.

For those looking to make healthier choices, the lower sugar variant offers a great compromise. No matter which version you choose, Kellogg's Coco Pops are a delightful way to start your day.


Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)


Are Kellogg's Coco Pops healthy?

While they are fortified with vitamins and minerals, they should be enjoyed as part of a balanced diet.


What makes Kellogg's Coco Pops different from other chocolate cereals?

The unique chocolatey taste and crunchy texture set them apart from other brands.


Is there a low sugar version of Kellogg's Coco Pops?

Yes, Kellogg's offers a version with 30% less sugar, catering to those looking for healthier options.


Can adults enjoy Kellogg's Coco Pops?

Absolutely! The nostalgic taste and satisfying crunch appeal to both kids and adults.
